title: Pulled from the water — check the breathing first
applies_to: Someone who has been under water and is now out of it, whether or not they are awake.

citations.source: European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: Basic Life Support
WHO and IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
International Life Saving Federation, Statement on Resuscitation of the Drowning Victim

steps.text: Look before you move. If going in would put you in danger, stay on land and reach or throw something out to them.
Call for help now, or shout for someone else to call while you work.
Once they are out of the water, tap their shoulders and shout. Look at the chest for up to 10 seconds.
If the chest is not rising and falling normally, lay them flat on their back on hard ground.
Tilt their head back, lift the chin, pinch the nose shut, and blow into the mouth 5 times. Each blow takes about 1 second and should make the chest rise.
Then put the heel of one hand in the middle of the chest and press straight down hard, about 5 cm deep, about 2 presses every second. Keep going.
If they are breathing normally, roll them onto their side so water and sick can drain out of the mouth.
Get them out of wet clothes if you can, and cover them to keep them warm.
Make sure a doctor sees them even if they now seem completely fine. Water in the chest can cause trouble hours later.

do_not: Do not press on the belly or hold them upside down to get water out. It does not work, and it makes them sick.
Do not go into deep, cold, or fast water to reach them unless you are trained for it.
Do not stop pushing on the chest because they look grey or feel cold.
Do not let them walk home alone afterwards.
Do not send anyone into the water alone. One person drowning becomes two that way.
escalate_if: They cough, wheeze, or breathe fast later in the day — get them to a doctor at once.
They were in cold water for a long time — keep pushing on the chest, and tell the crew how long they were in.
You cannot get them out of the water — keep their face above the water and wait for trained help.
They dived in, or fell from a height — treat the neck as hurt and try not to bend it.
